example.user: what's the normal adult dose of ibuprofen in mg, and how many times a day can you take it?
example.reply: For adults, ibuprofen is typically taken in doses of **200-400 mg** at a time, **every 4-6 hours as needed**. The maximum daily dose is usually **1200 mg in 24 hours** for over-the-counter use (without a doctor's guidance). **Important things to remember:** - Always take it with food or milk to reduce stomach irritation - Don't exceed the maximum daily dose - Use the lowest dose that works for you - Follow the instructions on the label or ask a pharmacist if you're unsure **When to avoid ibuprofen or check with a doctor first:** - History of stomach ulcers or bleeding problems - Heart disease, high blood pressure, or kidney problems - Already taking blood thinners or certain other medications - Asthma that worsens with NSAIDs - Pregnancy (especially third trimester) Is this for you, Rahul? If you're dealing with pain or fever, I'm happy to ask a few questions to see how you're doing.

examples.user: how much paracetamol syrup can I give my 3 year old, and how often?
examples.reply: For paracetamol (acetaminophen) syrup for Riya, who is 3 years old: **Dosing guidance:** - The dose depends on her **weight** (not just age). The usual dose is **15 mg per kg** of body weight - Can be given **every 4-6 hours** as needed - **Maximum 4 doses** in 24 hours - Always check the strength on your bottle (usually 120 mg/5 ml or 250 mg/5 ml in India) — the amount to give in ml will vary **I recommend:** 1. Check the dosing instructions on the label of your specific syrup 2. If unsure, ask a pharmacist — they can calculate the exact ml amount based on Riya's weight and your syrup's strength 3. Use the measuring cup or syringe that comes with the medicine for accuracy **When to see a doctor:** - Fever lasting more than 3 days - High fever (above 39°C/102°F) - Riya is very drowsy, not drinking, has a rash, difficulty breathing, or seems very unwell - Fever in a child always needs attention if you're worried Is Riya unwell right now? I can ask a few questions to see how she's doing and whether she needs to see a doctor.

example.user: for the past week I get a tight feeling in my chest when I climb stairs, it goes away when I rest
example.reply: Rajiv, chest tightness that comes on with exertion like climbing stairs and goes away with rest is an important symptom that needs medical evaluation soon. **What it might be:** This pattern can be a sign of angina (reduced blood flow to the heart muscle), especially given your age and family history of early heart disease. It could also be caused by other conditions like chest muscle strain or reflux, but the exertion-relief pattern is concerning for a heart issue. **What to do now:** Please see a doctor within the next 1-2 days, ideally your GP or a cardiologist. They will likely want to examine you, possibly do an ECG, and may arrange further tests. Don't wait for it to get worse. Avoid strenuous activity until you've been assessed. **Seek urgent care immediately (call emergency services or go to A&E) if you develop:** - Chest pain or pressure that is severe, lasts more than a few minutes, or doesn't go away with rest - Chest discomfort spreading to your arm, jaw, neck, or back - Shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, or feeling faint along with chest symptoms - Any chest symptoms that feel different or worse than what you've been experiencing This is not a diagnosis—you need a proper examination and tests to work out what's causing this.

examples.reply: Myra is only 5 months old and has a fever, so she should be seen by a doctor today. Babies under 6 months with fever need to be checked to rule out serious infections. **What you should do now:** - Take Myra to see a doctor today (your pediatrician if available, or an urgent care clinic/emergency department). - Keep offering breast or bottle feeds frequently to prevent dehydration, even if she's taking less. - Dress her in light clothing and keep the room comfortably cool. - Do **not** give any fever medicines without asking the doctor first, as dosing for infants this young needs to be carefully checked. **Seek urgent care immediately if Myra develops any of these warning signs:** - Temperature 100.4°F (38°C) or higher if she were under 3 months, but at 5 months any persistent fever needs checking today - Unusually sleepy, floppy, or hard to wake - Refusing feeds completely or not having wet nappies - Breathing fast or with difficulty - A rash that doesn't fade when you press a glass against it - Crying inconsolably or very high-pitched cry - Soft spot on her head bulging out This is not a diagnosis — the doctor will examine Myra to find out what's causing the fever.

At 48 years old, this needs urgent evaluation right now. **What to do immediately:** - Call for an ambulance or have someone take you to the hospital emergency department - If you have aspirin available and are not allergic, chew one 300mg tablet (or equivalent) while waiting for help - Stop any activity and sit or lie down in a comfortable position - Loosen any tight clothing - Do not eat or drink anything Time is critical with heart problems. twin_examples.reply: **CALL YOUR LOCAL EMERGENCY NUMBER (108 OR 112) OR GO TO THE NEAREST EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT IMMEDIATELY.** Face drooping and slurred speech are classic warning signs of a **stroke**, which is a medical emergency. With stroke, every minute matters — immediate treatment can save brain tissue and improve recovery. **What to do RIGHT NOW:** - Call an ambulance or get Ramesh to the nearest hospital emergency department immediately - Note the time the symptoms started (about 11:10 AM) — doctors will ask this - Do not give him anything to eat or drink - Keep him calm and lying down with his head slightly elevated - If he becomes unconscious, place him in the recovery position (on his side) **Why this is urgent:** At 74 years old with sudden face drooping and slurred speech, this is a stroke until proven otherwise. Treatment is most effective within the first few hours. Please act immediately and don't wait to see if it gets better. Call for emergency help now.
